newsitem.title: UK: ALUMINIUM BULL MARKET OPEN TO DOUBT - MERRILL.
newsitem.headline: ALUMINIUM BULL MARKET OPEN TO DOUBT - MERRILL.

text.p: Aluminium's bull run is not fully supported by fundamentals and will be prone to heavy fund profit-taking and forward selling by producers gearing up to restart idled capacity, broker Merrill Lynch said in a report.
"Our own view is that virtually all of the bullish comment being heard these days from brokers, funds and producers is very misleading," metals analyst Ted Arnold said.
"We think prices will be forced higher in the short term but the price strength will be utilised by producers as a forward selling opportunity," he added.
London Metal Exchange three month prices surged to fresh 22-month highs in early inter-office business on Thursday morning, hitting a peak of $1,762 per tonne.
This is a rise of $200 or 13 percent over the past three weeks.
Some players are targeting $1,800 and above, but Arnold said the fundamentals do not support such heady prices.
Stocks have been steadily falling, but a squeeze developing in August dates could attract metal into warehouses.
"A big backwardation could develop and suck in much more metal that is currently off-warrant or being held as consignment stock by semi-fabricators and consumers generally," Arnold said.
In addition, consumers are unlikely to continue the high level of stock-building seen during the first half of the year and a supply surplus is likely to develop in the second half.
Even the big hedge funds, which have been helping to fuel the rise, are becoming less certain about the future outlook.

"Some of them have indicated behind the scenes that they are no longer as bullish as they were about the macro-economic outlook for the Western world economy next year and thus the likely levels of aluminium consumption," the report said.
"Their mood suggests they are growing restless with their longs. They want to get out but preferably in a volume market with fresh buyers falling over themselves to buy their sales," Arnold added.
Lastly, producers are keen on a bull market and would see it as an opportunity to sell forward large amounts of metal at $1,675 and $1,700 per tonne basis 1998 and 1999 dates.

"It may be that those producers still sitting on idled capacity see this coming rally as an opportunity to sell forward and reactivate their capacity without damaging the aluminium price too much," the report said.
"We could be in for some very volatile trading ahead. Remember the old adage - A market is never so weak as when it looks its strongest."
